{{Short description|Concept in differential equation mathematics}}
{{no footnotes|date=June 2017}}
In [[mathematics]], in the theory of [[ordinary differential equation]]s in the [[complex plane]] <math>\Complex</math>, the points of <math>\Complex</math> are classified into ''ordinary points'', at which the equation's coefficients are [[analytic function]]s, and ''singular points'', at which some coefficient has a [[Singularity (mathematics)|singularity]]. Then amongst singular points, an important distinction is made between a '''regular singular point''', where the growth of solutions is bounded (in any small sector) by an [[algebraic function]], and an '''irregular singular point''', where the full [[solution set]] requires functions with higher growth rates. This distinction occurs, for example, between the [[hypergeometric equation]], with three regular singular points, and the [[Bessel equation]] which is in a sense a [[limiting case (mathematics)|limiting case]], but where the analytic properties are substantially different.

==Formal definitions==
More precisely, consider an ordinary [[linear differential equation]] of {{mvar|n}}-th order
<!--- :''Lf'' = Σ ''p''<sub>''i''</sub> (''z'')''f''<sup>(''i'')</sup>(''z'') = 0 --->
<math display="block"> f^{(n)}(z) + \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} p_i(z) f^{(i)} (z) = 0 </math>
with {{math|''p''<sub>''i''</sub>(''z'')}} [[meromorphic functions]].

The equation should be studied on the [[Riemann sphere]] to include the [[point at infinity]] as a possible singular point. A [[Möbius transformation]] may be applied to move ∞ into the finite part of the complex plane if required, see example on Bessel differential equation below.

Then the [[Frobenius method]] based on the [[indicial equation]] may be applied to find possible solutions that are [[power series]] times complex powers {{math|(''z'' − ''a'')<sup>''r''</sup>}} near any given {{mvar|a}} in the complex plane where {{mvar|r}} need not be an integer; this function may exist, therefore, only thanks to a [[branch cut]] extending out from {{mvar|a}}, or on a [[Riemann surface]] of some [[punctured disc]] around {{mvar|a}}. This presents no difficulty for {{mvar|a}} an ordinary point ([[Lazarus Fuchs]] 1866). When {{mvar|a}} is a '''regular singular point''', which by definition means that<!--- :''p''<sub>''n'' − ''i''</sub> (''z'') --->
<math display="block">p_{n-i}(z)</math>has a [[pole (complex analysis)|pole]] of order at most {{mvar|i}} at {{mvar|a}}, the [[Frobenius method]] also can be made to work and provide {{mvar|n}} independent solutions near {{mvar|a}}.

Otherwise the point {{mvar|a}} is an '''irregular singularity'''. In that case the [[monodromy group]] relating solutions by [[analytic continuation]] has less to say in general, and the solutions are harder to study, except in terms of their asymptotic expansions. The irregularity of an irregular singularity is measured by the [[Henri Poincaré|Poincaré]] rank.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Arscott |first=F. M. |title=Heun's Differential Equations |date=1995 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=0198596952 |editor-last=Ronveaux |editor-first=A. |pages=74 |chapter=Heun's Equation}}</ref>

The regularity condition is a kind of [[Newton polygon]] condition, in the sense that the allowed poles are in a region, when plotted against {{var|i}}, bounded by a line at 45° to the axes.

An [[ordinary differential equation]] whose only singular points, including the point at infinity, are regular singular points is called a '''[[Fuchsian theory|Fuchsian]]'''{{anchor|Fuchsian differential equation}} ordinary differential equation.

==Examples for second order differential equations==
In this case the equation above is reduced to:
<math display="block">f''(x) + p_1(x) f'(x) + p_0(x) f(x) = 0. </math>

One distinguishes the following cases:
*Point {{mvar|a}} is an  '''ordinary point''' when functions {{math|''p''<sub>1</sub>(''x'')}} and {{math|''p''<sub>0</sub>(''x'')}} are analytic at {{math|1=''x'' = ''a''}}.
*Point {{mvar|a}} is a '''regular singular point''' if {{math|''p''<sub>1</sub>(''x'')}} has a pole up to order 1 at {{math|1=''x'' = ''a''}} and {{math|''p''<sub>0</sub>}} has a pole of order up to 2 at {{math|1=''x'' = ''a''}}.
*Otherwise point {{mvar|a}} is an '''irregular singular point'''.

We can check whether there is an irregular singular point at infinity by using the substitution <math>w = 1/x</math> and the relations:
<math display="block">\frac{df}{dx}=-w^2\frac{df}{dw}</math>
<math display="block">\frac{d^2f}{dx^2}=w^4\frac{d^2f}{dw^2}+2w^3\frac{df}{dw}</math>

We can thus transform the equation to an equation in {{mvar|w}}, and check what happens at {{math|1=''w'' = 0}}. If <math>p_1(x)</math> and <math>p_2(x)</math> are quotients of polynomials, then there will be an irregular singular point at infinite ''x'' unless the polynomial in the denominator of <math>p_1(x)</math> is of [[degree of a polynomial|degree]] at least one more than the degree of its numerator and the denominator of <math>p_2(x)</math> is of degree at least two more than the degree of its numerator.

Listed below are several examples from ordinary differential equations from [[mathematical physics]] that have singular points and known solutions.

===Bessel differential equation===
This is an ordinary differential equation of second order. It is found in the solution to [[Laplace's equation]] in [[cylindrical coordinates]]:
<math display="block">x^2 \frac{d^2 f}{dx^2} + x \frac{df}{dx} + (x^2 - \alpha^2)f = 0</math>
for an arbitrary real or [[complex number]] {{mvar|α}} (the ''order'' of the [[Bessel function]]). The most common and important special case is where {{mvar|α}} is an [[integer]] {{mvar|n}}.

Dividing this equation by ''x''<sup>2</sup> gives:
<math display="block">\frac{d^2 f}{dx^2} + \frac{1} {x} \frac{df}{dx} + \left (1 - \frac {\alpha^2} {x^2} \right )f = 0.</math>

In this case {{math|1=''p''<sub>1</sub>(''x'') = 1/''x''}} has a pole of first order at {{math|1=''x'' = 0}}. When {{math|''α'' ≠ 0}}, {{math|1=''p''<sub>0</sub>(''x'') = (1 − ''α''<sup>2</sup>/''x''<sup>2</sup>)}} has a pole of second order at {{math|1=''x'' = 0}}. Thus this equation has a regular singularity at 0.

To see what happens when {{math|''x'' → ∞}} one has to use a [[Möbius transformation]], for example <math>x = 1 / w</math>. After performing the algebra:
<math display="block">\frac{d^2 f}{d w^2} + \frac{1}{w} \frac{df}{dw} + 
\left[ \frac{1}{w^4} - \frac{\alpha ^2}{w^2} \right ] f= 0
</math>

Now at {{nowrap|<math>w = 0</math>,}}
<math display="block">p_1(w) = \frac{1}{w}</math>
has a pole of first order, but
<math display="block">p_0(w) = \frac {1} {w^4} - \frac {\alpha ^2} {w^2}</math>
has a pole of fourth order. Thus, this equation has an irregular singularity at <math>w = 0</math> corresponding to ''x'' at ∞.

===Legendre differential equation===
This is an ordinary differential equation of second order. It is found in the solution of [[Laplace's equation]] in [[spherical coordinates]]:
<math display="block">\frac{d}{dx} \left[ (1-x^2) \frac{d}{dx} f \right] + \ell(\ell+1)f = 0.</math>

Opening the square bracket gives:
<math display="block">\left(1-x^2\right){d^2 f \over dx^2} -2x {df \over dx } + \ell(\ell+1)f = 0.</math>

And dividing by {{math|(1 − ''x''<sup>2</sup>)}}:
<math display="block">\frac{d^2 f}{dx^2} - \frac{2x}{1-x^2} \frac{df}{dx} + \frac{\ell(\ell+1)}{1-x^2} f = 0.</math>

This differential equation has regular singular points at ±1 and ∞.

===Hermite differential equation===
One encounters this ordinary second order differential equation in solving the one-dimensional time independent [[Schrödinger equation]]
<math display="block">E\psi = -\frac{\hbar^2}{2m} \frac {d^2 \psi} {d x^2} + V(x)\psi</math>
for a [[Quantum harmonic oscillator|harmonic oscillator]]. In this case the potential energy ''V''(''x'') is:
<math display="block"> V(x) = \frac{1}{2} m \omega^2 x^2.</math>

This leads to the following ordinary second order differential equation:
<math display="block">\frac{d^2 f}{dx^2} - 2 x \frac{df}{dx} + \lambda f = 0.</math>

This differential equation has an irregular singularity at ∞. Its solutions are [[Hermite polynomials]].

===Hypergeometric equation===
The equation may be defined as
<math display="block">z(1-z)\frac {d^2f}{dz^2} + \left[c-(a+b+1)z \right] \frac {df}{dz} - abf = 0.</math>

Dividing both sides by {{math|''z''(1 − ''z'')}} gives:
<math display="block">\frac {d^2f}{dz^2} + \frac{c-(a+b+1)z } {z(1-z)} \frac {df}{dz} - \frac {ab} {z(1-z)} f = 0.</math>

This differential equation has regular singular points at 0, 1 and ∞. A solution is the [[hypergeometric function]].
